title: Saudi Arabia exits China-led mBridge currency platform in blow to de-dollarization push
excerpt: Riyadh's central bank says it completed its proof of concept in May 2025 and never intended to stay; the quiet exit, reported by the Financial Times, removes the world's top oil exporter from a system built to sidestep the dollar.
body:
• The Saudi Central Bank (SAMA) confirmed to the Financial Times it ceased being an mBridge participant after completing its minimum viable product proof of concept on May 13, 2025; the withdrawal had never been made public.
  • SAMA joined as an observing member in 2023 under the Bank for International Settlements and became a full participant in June 2024, giving Riyadh a front-row view of the technology without committing to commercial use.
  • mBridge uses distributed ledger technology to let central banks settle directly in their own digital currencies, cutting foreign-exchange costs and reducing the dollar's role as an intermediary; the platform has reportedly processed more than $55 billion in transactions.
  • The exit follows the BIS's own departure in October 2024 and arrives as Washington scrutinizes whether the platform could help sanctioned states bypass dollar-based systems like SWIFT.

Saudi Arabia has quietly withdrawn from mBridge, the China-led digital currency platform built to settle cross-border payments outside the dollar-based financial system, the Financial Times reported. The Saudi Central Bank, known as SAMA, confirmed the departure and said it had completed its proof of concept on May 13, 2025, describing the exit as consistent with its original plan rather than a sudden policy reversal.

The disclosure ends more than a year of ambiguity about Riyadh's role in the project. SAMA first joined mBridge as an observing member in 2023 under the umbrella of the Bank for International Settlements, then upgraded to full participant status in June 2024 and helped develop the platform's basic working version. A source familiar with the matter told the FT that SAMA no longer wants to be publicly linked to the project but continues to engage with it discreetly. Another source cautioned against overreading the move, saying Riyadh's role was limited from the start.

Context & Background

Project mBridge began in 2021 as an experiment by the BIS Innovation Hub, the People's Bank of China, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Bank of Thailand and the Central Bank of the United Arab Emirates. Built on distributed ledger technology, it allows participating institutions to transact directly in central bank digital currencies, trimming the time and cost of foreign-exchange settlement and removing the dollar as the default intermediary.

The platform has moved beyond experimentation. Reuters reported in January that mBridge had processed more than $55 billion in transactions, and the remaining members are preparing a commercial rollout under a new Hong Kong-based entity. The Monetary Authority of Macau joined the project this year and launched the system in June. The BIS itself stepped back in October 2024; its then general manager, Agustín Carstens, said the institution had "graduated out" and that politics played no part, though reports at the time said Washington had pressed it to leave.

Impact & Analysis

The departure strips mBridge of its most symbolically important participant. Saudi Arabia is the world's largest crude oil exporter, and the prospect of Riyadh settling oil in digital yuan or other non-dollar currencies was central to the platform's challenge to the petrodollar system. With the kingdom out, Saudi energy settlements remain anchored to traditional dollar-denominated plumbing for the foreseeable future.

The move also reflects Riyadh's balancing act. The kingdom deepens trade ties with Beijing while preserving its security alliance with Washington, which has openly worried that platforms like mBridge could let sanctioned nations circumvent dollar-based payment networks such as SWIFT. SAMA's framing — an exploratory exercise that ran its course — lets Riyadh keep a foot in the technology without crossing a geopolitical line.

"It would be inaccurate to read a wider meaning into the decision, as Riyadh's role was limited from the start."

— A source familiar with the matter, via the Financial Times

Market reaction is likely to be measured rather than dramatic: the exit formalizes a status quo that has been in place since May 2025. But symbolically, the loss of both the BIS and Saudi Arabia within two years undercuts the narrative that mBridge is on a glide path to becoming a genuine parallel to the dollar system.

Diaspora Angle

For the millions of Indian workers in the Gulf who send money home, the plumbing of cross-border settlement matters directly — a shift to digital-currency rails could one day reshape remittance costs and corridors. Saudi Arabia's exit signals that the dollar-denominated networks those transfers run on will remain dominant for now.

What's Next

mBridge's remaining members — China, Hong Kong, Thailand, the UAE and now Macau — continue developing the platform toward commercial use, and its transaction volumes give it real traction independent of Riyadh. The open questions are whether the platform attracts a major commodity exporter to replace Saudi Arabia's symbolic weight, and how the United States responds as the system scales. For now, the dollar's grip on global settlement looks intact — but Beijing's alternative rails keep being built.
